Your first salary lands on the 1st. By the 20th, you are checking your balance and wondering where it went.

Nobody explains what to do with a real salary. HR wants your tax regime before a deadline. A colleague mentions a SIP. Your parents ask if you have started saving. You open a spreadsheet and drop it by Sunday.

Meanwhile rent, the EMI on the new phone and weekend plans take their share first, and whatever survives gets called savings. A year in, there is no emergency fund, no investment, and a tax regime picked in a hurry.

The First Salary Playbook walks you through these decisions in the order they arrive, in plain English and in rupees.

What you will be able to do:
  • Split your salary on the day it arrives, so rent and bills are covered and the rest is not left to willpower
  • Build an emergency fund and work out the exact amount you need from your own monthly expenses
  • Start your first SIP with an amount you can keep paying even in a bad month
  • Put the old and new tax regimes side by side using your own payslip, and choose the one that leaves more in your hand
  • Spot the small leaks that quietly eat a month: forgotten subscriptions, gadget EMIs and the last-week food-delivery spree
Written by a Bengaluru chartered accountant who explains each step the way you would to a friend, with worked examples you can copy.

It will not make you rich by thirty. It will make sure your first salary starts working for you from month one.

If you are 22 to 28, newly employed and still have no plan, this book is for you. Start reading today.

samples.text:
KEYNOTE: "THE ROAD, NOT THE FIELD"
Speaker: founder, Nagpur cold-chain logistics company. Slot: 12 minutes. Delivery copy. [PAUSE] marks one full breath. Hindi lines are in Roman script, written as they are spoken.

[OPENING]

Good morning, friends. I will keep my thank-yous for the end, because I want to start with a gate. [PAUSE]

Two o'clock in the morning. A mandi gate. [PAUSE]

You have stood there. Some of you were the farmer in this picture. Some of you were the one with the clipboard. A truck of green peas has been in the queue since eleven. The farmer's son is asleep on the sacks. Those peas were picked yesterday afternoon, when they were perfect. Firm, sweet, the best that field could give.

[PAUSE]

Now it is two a.m. The sun will be up in four hours. The price of those peas will be decided by what four more hours of heat do to them. Not by anything that farmer did right in the last four months.

Mehnat kheton mein hoti hai. Nuksaan raaste mein.

[PAUSE]

[THE BIG IDEA]

I run refrigerated trucks out of Nagpur. I have come here this morning to say one sentence. Please carry it into lunch and say it to the person beside you.

[PAUSE]

Farm waste is a logistics problem before it is a farming problem.

[PAUSE]

Say it again, quietly, to yourself. Farm waste is a logistics problem before it is a farming problem.

[SIGNPOST]

Three things today. The clock. The gap. And the shed. Each one is short. By the end you will know what I am asking of you. It will cost five minutes of your day, not five crore of your budget.

[MOVE ONE: THE CLOCK]

Let me start with the clock.

Let me describe a farmer. He is not one man. He is a composite of many I could name, and he would forgive me for not naming him. He did everything the agriculture officer told him. Right seed. Right water. Right spray, right week. He harvested on the right morning, at the right stage, and he graded his crop by hand.

Then he waited for a truck.

[PAUSE]

Here is what nobody puts in the scheme document. A crop does not ask what the rate is. It asks what time it is. The moment a vegetable or a fruit is cut, a clock starts. It does not stop for the festival, for the transporter who is late, or for the mandi that opens at five.

Here is the one number I want you to keep from this part. On the routes my company has run, the wait between harvest and the first cold air is [client number: median hours, rounded, with route and season]. Not days. Hours. And in those hours the produce is already losing what the farmer worked for.

We keep blaming the field. We run training on seed and soil. Good. Needed. But the best seed in Vidarbha cannot beat a ten-hour wait in the sun.

[PAUSE]

So the first thing I want to move in your minds is this. Do not ask only how well the crop was grown. Ask how long it waited. [PAUSE] Quality is grown in the field, but it is kept, or lost, on the road.

[MOVE TWO: THE GAP]

Now the gap.

There is a gap in the middle of every farm-to-market story. On one side is the farm gate. On the other side is the buyer's cold room. In between there is a stretch of road, a stretch of time, and no refrigeration at all. The farmer's work ends at one side. The buyer's responsibility begins at the other. And in the gap, nobody's name is on the produce. [PAUSE]

I know the question this room is already asking, because I would ask it too. Why don't we build our own cold room? Every FPO should have one. [PAUSE]

It is a fair question, so let me answer it honestly.

A cold room is built for the peak and paid for all year. An FPO harvests in bursts. A few weeks of rush, then months of a half-empty room and a full electricity bill. [PAUSE] The room looks wonderful in the photograph at the inauguration. It is a loss in the ledger by the second year.

[founder story: one sentence on a cold room you saw sitting empty, or a first load you lost, and what it taught you]

And bankers, I am speaking to you now. You have been told, rightly, that a cold room that sits empty is a poor loan. I agree with you. A room that belongs to one FPO and one crop will sit empty. [PAUSE] But a room that five FPOs share, whose harvest weeks fall at different times, does not. The same compressor, the same building, the same power connection, and a different crop moving through it in every season. That is not a risk to be priced out. That is a utility waiting to be shared.

Alone, a cold room is a cost. Shared, it is a road.

[PAUSE]

Beej hum saath bote hain. Mandi mein akele khade hote hain. Thande ka kharcha phir saath baant sakte hain.

[PAUSE]

[MOVE THREE: THE SHED]

Which brings me to the shed.

I do not mean a grand building. I mean a shed, near your village or your block, where your crates arrive in the afternoon and the cold begins the same evening. A shed with a thermometer on the wall that anyone can read. A shed where the produce of several FPOs sits under one roof, each in its own marked crates, each counted in and counted out.

Go back to the gate at two a.m. [PAUSE] Now put the same peas in a crate at four in the afternoon. In the shed by six. Cold by eight that evening. [PAUSE] They rest through the night, and the farmer's son rests too, at home. At nine the next morning a buyer opens a crate in daylight and sees what the farmer grew. Not what the road did to it.

That is a different conversation about price. It is a conversation the farmer can win.

And look at what else the shed does. A graded, counted, cold crate is something a banker can see. Something a processor can plan a shift around. Something an FPO leader can show a member and say: this is yours, and this is where it is.

The farmer has the crop. The FPO has the trust. The banker has the credit. The processor has the order. The cold shed is the one piece that was missing, and it is the one piece no single one of us can afford alone.

[PAUSE]

[THE TURN: IF WE ACT, AND IF WE DO NOT]

Let me put it plainly, because I respect this room too much to be vague.

If we do nothing, next season will look like last season. The same photographs. The same tomatoes on the highway, the same peas at the same gate at two a.m., a different year on the calendar. The same farmer will do everything right and take home the least. And when that farmer asks who failed him, he will not blame the road. He will blame his FPO.

[PAUSE]

If we act, even small, even in one district, there will be one place in this region by the next harvest. A place where a farmer can bring his crop at the end of the day and know that tonight, at least, the clock has stopped.

Not all waste will go. I will not stand here and promise you that. But some of it will, and that some belongs to the person who worked the hardest and was paid the least.

[PAUSE]

[THE ASK]

So here is what I am asking. One thing.

FPO leaders, before you leave this hall today, come to our stall. Write three things on the pilot sheet: your FPO's name, your main crop, and the month your harvest peaks. [PAUSE] That is all. It is not a contract. It is not a payment. It is a name, a crop and a month.

With enough names from nearby districts, whose harvest months do not overlap, we can plan one shared cold-storage pilot [pilot site and start month: client to confirm]. One season will tell us whether this works. If it does not, you will have lost five minutes. If it does, your members will have a shed.

Bankers, come and look at the sheet, and tell me what you would need to see to finance the second shed. Processors, tell me which crates you want first.

[PAUSE]

[CLOSE]

Let me take you back, one last time, to that gate.

Two o'clock in the morning. A mandi gate. [PAUSE]

Next season, let it be quiet. Let the queue be short, because nothing had to wait. Let the farmer's son sleep in his own bed, not on the sacks. Let the peas already be cold, in a shed, near home, counted and marked with his father's name.

[PAUSE]

Kheti ko raasta chahiye. Chaliye, raasta banate hain.

[PAUSE]

Farm waste is a logistics problem before it is a farming problem. Let us solve the part that is ours to solve.

Thank you. Please do come by the stall.

How do I cancel an e-invoice I raised by mistake?

You can cancel an e-invoice from the web app within 24 hours of generating it. After 24 hours the invoice cannot be cancelled, and you correct it with a credit note instead.

Before you start
- Your login needs the Owner or Accountant role.
- If goods have left with an e-way bill, cancel the e-way bill first. The app will not cancel an e-invoice while its e-way bill is active.

Steps (web app)
1. Sign in and open **Sales**, then **E-invoices**.
2. Type the invoice number in **Search invoices** and open the invoice.
3. Check **IRN generated** at the top of the page. Cancellation is possible only within 24 hours of that time.
4. Click **More actions**, then **Cancel e-invoice**.
5. Pick a reason from **Reason for cancellation**. Choose **Data entry mistake** if you raised the invoice in error.
6. Type a short remark, such as "Wrong customer GSTIN", and click **Confirm cancellation**.
7. Wait for the status to change from **Active** to **Cancelled**. If it still shows **Active** after one minute, refresh the page.

Screenshot 1
Alt text: Invoice detail page with the IRN generated time highlighted at the top and the More actions menu open, showing Cancel e-invoice.
Caption: Check the IRN generated time first. If it is more than 24 hours old, Cancel e-invoice is greyed out.

Screenshot 2
Alt text: Cancel e-invoice dialog with Reason for cancellation set to Data entry mistake, a remark typed in, and the Confirm cancellation button.
Caption: Pick the reason that matches what happened.

If you see "The cancellation window has passed for this invoice"
The 24 hours are over, so the original invoice stays on record. Do this instead:
1. Open the invoice, click **More actions**, then **Create credit note**.
2. Select **Full invoice value** and confirm. The app generates an e-invoice for the credit note.
3. Raise the corrected invoice under **Sales**, then **New invoice**.
4. Tell your accountant. The invoice and its credit note both appear in your GSTR-1 for that month.

If you see "E-way bill is active for this invoice"
Open **Sales**, then **E-way bills**, open the bill and click **Cancel e-way bill**. Then repeat steps 4 to 7 above.

Related articles
- How do I create a credit note for an e-invoice?
- How do I cancel an e-way bill?
- How do I correct a wrong customer GSTIN?

Still stuck?
Open **Help**, then **Contact support**. Include the invoice number and a screenshot of the error. Never share your password or an OTP with anyone, including our support team.

HEADLINE
What changed when we moved 40 karigars from piece-rate to a monthly salary

COVER IMAGE
[photo: client's own, a karigar at a processing table in the Surat unit, taken with consent]
Alt text: Close view of a karigar's hands guiding printed fabric across a finishing table in a textile processing unit.

LEDE
We moved 40 karigars from piece-rate to a monthly salary. Attrition went from [attrition before] to [attrition after]. Rework went from [rework before] to [rework after]. Output per karigar [rose / fell / held] by [output change].

That is the short version. The long version has a cost I did not plan for and two things I got wrong, so I will tell you all three.

WHY NOW
For years I treated attrition as the weather in Surat's processing belt. A skilled hand leaves for a unit paying a little more per piece, and you hire again. What changed was the lot that came back from a buyer: [the trigger, from your records: month, lot size, what the buyer rejected]. When I added up what we had paid to make that lot twice, I stopped calling it weather. A skilled karigar is not hard to find in Surat. One who stays long enough to learn your buyer's standards is.

WHAT PIECE-RATE WAS REALLY PAYING FOR

Piece-rate paid for speed, and we paid for the same piece twice.

A karigar on piece-rate is paid for what leaves the table. Nothing is paid for what comes back. So the sensible thing for him to do, and I would have done the same, is to finish the lot and let the checker find the fault. By the time the fault was found, [what happened next in your unit: re-run, re-dye, re-finish] had to be paid for again, often at overtime.

Our own records showed the pattern. Before the change, rework was [rework before], measured as [your measure: lots, metres or pieces] over [period]. I had never added it to the wage bill, because piece-rate wages looked clean on paper: no output, no payment. The cost was just hidden in another column.

WHAT THE SALARY LOOKS LIKE

A salary only works if you price the floor correctly.

Set it too low and your best hands leave in the first month. Set it too high and you have bought idle time. We fixed ours by [how the monthly amount was set: for example from each karigar's past earnings, by skill grade; client to supply]. Attendance rules: [rules]. Overtime: [rules]. A quality bonus: [yes or no, and how it is measured].

The part that surprised me was not the amount. It was the conversation. When we announced the change, [karigar reaction, in your words or theirs, with permission]. For the first time, someone on the floor told me about a machine problem before the lot was ruined, because there was nothing to lose by saying it.

WHAT IT COST US

It was not free. A salary is a fixed cost, and slack months arrive whether you have orders or not. Our wage bill moved from [wage bill before] to [wage bill after] a month. In [slack month or period] we carried [the number or the gap] of idle capacity and paid for it.

What paid for it was [what offset it: rework saved, fewer rehires, fewer rejected lots, in rupees, from your records]. If you cannot find a similar offset in your own numbers, do not copy us.

HOW TO READ THESE NUMBERS

Treat them as one unit's result, not a rule. They cover [period measured] and 40 people. [Other changes in the same period: new supervisor, buyer or machine.] I cannot separate the effect of the salary from those changes, and anyone who says they can is selling something.

WHAT I GOT WRONG

I got two things wrong.

First, [mistake one: for example, I assumed everyone wanted a salary. Fill from the real story]. Second, [mistake two: for example, I changed pay but not how supervisors checked quality]. Both cost us [time or money]. We fixed them by [the change].

Monthly pay does not remove the need to check quality. It only removes the reason to hide a mistake.

THE TAKEAWAY: FIVE QUESTIONS BEFORE YOU TRY THIS
- Do you know your rework cost in rupees? If it is not on a page, start there.
- What is your slack-month cash cover? Count it in months of wages, not hopes.
- Who judges quality, and does he report to the karigars or to you?
- Which of your 40 would leave if you changed nothing?
- What will you do if the first quarter's numbers look worse? Decide before you start.

CLOSE
Back to that lot from the buyer. I do not think anyone on the floor was careless. We had paid them to be fast, and they were. Now we pay them to be right.

If you run a unit with piece-rate workers, tell me in the comments how you pay them and what has gone wrong. Then subscribe to this newsletter so the next edition reaches you.

samples.text:
# 9 documents salaried home-loan applicants in Pune forget (and how long each one delays approval)

If you are a salaried first-time buyer in Pune, this list is for you. Most home-loan files do not stall on credit score. They stall on a missing or mismatched paper, and the lender's query comes back days after you thought you were done.

We built the list from our home-loan ops team's notes on files that stalled [period and number of files: ops team to supply]. The items run in the order a file moves: income papers first, then credit, then the property. For each one you get why it matters, where to get it, and the delay we typically saw [delay figures: from the ops notes].

By the end you will know which papers to collect this weekend, so the lender's first question is not a surprise.

## The quick list

1. A bank statement from the account your salary actually lands in
2. Form 16, both parts
3. Your last two ITRs, with computation
4. An appointment or confirmation letter, if you changed jobs recently
5. A name that matches across PAN, Aadhaar and salary slips
6. Statements and NOCs for loans you already have
7. Your own credit report, read before the lender reads it
8. The registered agreement and Index II extract
9. Occupancy certificate, society NOC and 7/12, where they apply

### 1. A bank statement from the account your salary actually lands in

Applicants send the statement of the account they use daily. The lender wants to see salary credits, month after month, from your employer's name.

If the salary lands in one account and you spend from another, send the salary account. Six months is the usual ask, though some lenders ask for more.

Where to get it: net banking, as a PDF with the bank's header. Some lenders want a stamped copy from the branch.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 2. Form 16, both parts

Part B shows the salary break-up. Part A shows the tax your employer deposited. Many applicants have only one, or only the last month's salary slip.

Ask HR before you apply. Employers usually issue Form 16 after the financial year ends, so if you are applying in April or May, ask when it will be ready.

Where to get it: your employer's HR or payroll portal. Part A can also be downloaded by the employer from TRACES.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 3. Your last two ITRs, with computation

The acknowledgement page is not enough. Lenders usually want the filed return with the computation of income, so they can match it to Form 16.

If your return was filed by a family CA, ask for the full PDF, not a screenshot of the acknowledgement.

Where to get it: income tax e-filing portal, under "View Filed Returns".
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 4. An appointment or confirmation letter, if you changed jobs recently

If you joined your employer a few months ago, or are still on probation, the lender will want proof that the job is confirmed. The salary slip does not say this.

Ask HR for a confirmation letter that states your designation, date of joining and fixed salary. One paragraph is enough.

Where to get it: HR, usually on the same working day if you ask directly.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 5. A name that matches across PAN, Aadhaar and salary slips

A missing initial, a married name, a spelling that differs by one letter. Small mismatches stall a file because the lender's system cannot link your records.

Check all four documents side by side before you apply. If one is wrong, correct it at the source, not on the loan form.

Where to get it fixed: PAN and Aadhaar corrections are done through the issuing authority's portal; carry the gazette notification or marriage certificate for a name change.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 6. Statements and NOCs for loans you already have

A car loan, a personal loan, a credit card balance. The lender will count every one of them against your repayment capacity.

If you plan to close a loan before you apply, get the foreclosure letter and NOC in writing. A closed loan the lender cannot see as closed is still counted.

Where to get it: the lender's app or branch. The NOC is usually issued after the final payment clears.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 7. Your own credit report, read before the lender reads it

Errors happen: a closed card shown as open, a loan that is not yours. You are better off finding them first.

Pull your report a few weeks before applying. If something is wrong, raise a dispute with the bureau and keep the reference number.

Where to get it: the credit bureau's website. You can usually download one free report a year.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 8. The registered agreement and Index II extract

For a Pune flat, the registered agreement for sale and its Index II extract are what the lender's legal team reads first. Buyers often have the agreement but not the extract.

If the flat is under construction, check the builder's registration details as well.

Where to get it: Maharashtra's registration department (IGR) website, or the sub-registrar's office where the agreement was registered.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

### 9. Occupancy certificate, society NOC and 7/12, where they apply

These depend on the property. A completed flat needs an occupancy certificate. A resale flat needs the society's NOC. A plot or a flat on land with a 7/12 extract needs the extract.

Ask the builder or the seller for whichever applies before you pay the token amount, not after.

Where to get it: the Pune Municipal Corporation or the relevant civic body for the occupancy certificate; the society office for the NOC; the Mahabhulekh portal for the 7/12 extract.
Typical delay if missing: [ops note: working days].

## Where to start

Start with item 1 today. Download your salary-account statement for the last six months and check that your employer's name appears on every credit. It takes ten minutes.

Then download our document checklist. It has all nine in one page, with a tick box for each, so you can walk into the lender's office with nothing missing.

Download the document checklist: [link]

Mid-Day Meals and School Attendance in India Since 2000: A Thematic Review

1. Introduction and scope

The mid-day meal programme is one of the largest school-based public programmes in the world. It began nationally in 1995, became a cooked-meal entitlement for primary school children through a Supreme Court order in 2001, and is now run as PM POSHAN. Bihar's education department and its funders are considering a new state pilot. They need to know what evidence already exists before they decide what the pilot should measure.

This review asks one question: what does the evidence since 2000 show about the effect of mid-day meals on school attendance in India, for which children, and under what conditions of delivery? It treats three further outcomes as part of the answer rather than as separate topics: nutrition, social equity and implementation quality. Each shapes whether a meal brings a child to school and keeps them there.

The review covers India only, from 2000 to the date of the report, and children in government and aided schools, Classes I to VIII.

Sources and method. The review is built only from the 25 studies and government evaluations supplied by [NGO name]. No independent database search was run, so a study absent from the supplied set is not evidence that none exists. Inclusion followed three rules: the source was published or issued since 2000, it is based on Indian data, and it reports an outcome on attendance, nutrition, social equity or implementation. [Writer to confirm: all 25 were read in full, not from abstracts, and each reference was checked against its DOI or report record].

2. Thematic sections

The four sections below each open with a claim slot, to be completed from the evidence. The first paragraph of each is written here; the remaining paragraphs follow the plan under it. Citations appear as slots because the supplied studies were not available to the writer, and no reference has been written from memory.

2.1 Attendance

The central question in the supplied evidence is whether a cooked meal changes who attends on a given day, as distinct from who is on the register. [Claim to complete: one sentence on the direction and size of the effect reported across the supplied studies, with a count of how many of the 25 agree]. Studies measure this in two ways: administrative records such as enrolment and registers, and household or school surveys of attendance (Author A, [year]; Author B, [year]). The two do not always agree. Registers can overstate attendance where a meal gives a reason to be marked present, and a survey captures only the day of the visit. Where the sources differ, the difference tracks [study design, state, period, or age group: writer to confirm] rather than the programme itself (Author C, [year]).

Plan for the rest of the section. (a) The studies with the strongest identification, and what they find. (b) Whether effects differ by sex, age and distance from school. (c) Whether effects appear at enrolment, daily attendance or dropout, and why these should not be pooled. (d) What this means for a pilot that must choose one attendance measure.

2.2 Nutrition

Mid-day meals are justified on both education and nutrition grounds, so this section asks what the supplied studies say about the link between the two. [Claim to complete: one sentence on what the nutrition studies show about intake, growth or anaemia, and whether any connect nutrition to attendance]. The nutrition evidence in the supplied set comes from [number of states and cohorts: writer to count] (Author D, [year]; Author E, [year]), which bears on how far it can be generalised to Bihar.

Plan. (a) The evidence on intake versus growth outcomes. (b) Whether children's meals at home change when a school meal is served. (c) The evidence on menu, quantity and frequency, and why a meal served on fewer days than due weakens any estimate.

2.3 Social equity

This section asks whether the effect on attendance is the same for every child, and what the supplied sources record about gains and frictions for particular groups. [Claim to complete: one sentence on which groups of children gain most, and what the sources report about caste, gender or religion in cooking, serving and seating]. Studies that examine the identity of the cook and the seating arrangement report [what they find: writer to complete from the sources] (Author F, [year]).

Plan. (a) Gender and enrolment. (b) Social-group differences in attendance and in access to the meal. (c) What the sources say about households that withdraw children when the meal arrangement is contested.

2.4 Implementation quality

This section asks how delivery varies: whether the meal is served on schedule, in the right quantity and in decent conditions, and whether that variation explains differences in findings. [Claim to complete: one sentence summarising how the government evaluations rate delivery and what they identify as the main failures]. Where government evaluations and independent studies diverge, the divergence reflects [reporting basis, sample or period: writer to confirm] (Author G, [year]; Government evaluation H, [year]).

RUN OF SHOW: [BRAND] BLOCK-PRINT SAREE LIVE

HEADER
Show: [Brand], Jaipur block-print sarees, festive launch live
Date and time: Saturday [date], 7:00 pm to 8:00 pm IST
Platforms: YouTube and Instagram, simulcast
Host: [Host name]. Guest: [Weaver name], weaver. Producer: [name]. Chat moderator: [name]
Products and codes: [link to the product page], codes [CODE1] and [CODE2]
Never put the stream key in this document. Producer keeps it separate.

PRE-SHOW CHECKLIST (6:00 to 7:00 pm)
[ ] 6:00 Guest on the call, camera and audio tested, backup phone hotspot ready
[ ] 6:10 Both platforms live in private mode, simulcast check, audio levels matched
[ ] 6:20 All 8 sarees laid out in order S1 to S8, each with its tag and stock count
[ ] 6:30 Stock counts typed into the shared sheet. Producer reads them back to the host
[ ] 6:40 Payment link tested with a Rs 1 order. Pinned comment text saved
[ ] 6:45 Moderator briefed: banned words, fabric-care FAQs, who answers price questions
[ ] 6:55 Lower thirds loaded: Flash 1, Flash 2, Stock left, Fabric care
[ ] 7:00 Go live

COLD OPEN (7:00 to 7:02, host)
- "Namaste, [Brand] live mein aapka swagat. Aaj 60 minute mein 8 block-print sarees dekhenge."
- "Pehla flash offer 7:18 pe, doosra 7:48 pe. Dono sirf 10 minute ke."
- "Beech mein hamare weaver [Name] se fabric care ke sawaal bhi puchh sakte hain."
- No waiting for people to join. Start with the sarees.

SEGMENT TABLE
| Start | Min | Segment | Speaks | On screen | CTA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7:00 | 2 | Cold open | Host | Brand card, agenda | None |
| 7:02 | 4 | Meet the weaver | Host, guest | Guest name tag | None |
| 7:06 | 12 | Sarees S1 to S4 | Host | Product tag, stock left | None |
| 7:18 | 10 | Flash offer 1 | Host | Flash 1 timer, stock | CTA 1 |
| 7:28 | 10 | Fabric-care Q&A | Guest, host | Fabric care lower third | None |
| 7:38 | 10 | Sarees S5 to S8 | Host | Product tag, stock left | None |
| 7:48 | 10 | Flash offer 2 | Host | Flash 2 timer, stock | CTA 2 |
| 7:58 | 2 | Close | Host | Recap card, next live | CTA 3 |

TALKING POINTS (bullets, not a script)

7:02 Meet the weaver (cut to 2 minutes if running long)
- [Weaver name] introduces themselves: how many years printing, which workshop
- How a block gets carved and stamped on the cloth, and why no two sarees match exactly
- How long one saree takes: [days, from the client]
- Cue to host: "Chaliye, ab sarees dekhte hain."

7:06 Sarees S1 to S4 (3 minutes each)
- For each: name, fabric, motif, colour, price, stock. Say the stock number aloud and point to the lower third.
- One styling idea per saree: office, wedding guest, festival day

- Cue: "Ab pehla flash offer shuru karte hain, aur sirf 10 minute ka hai."

7:18 Flash offer 1 (S1 to S4)
- Read the offer once, slowly, then repeat at 7:23
- Read stock left every 2 minutes from the shared sheet, never from memory
- Shout out buyers by first name from the order feed if they agreed
- Cue: "7:28 pe offer band. Ab weaver se fabric care ke sawaal."

7:28 Fabric-care Q&A (cut to 6 minutes if running long)
- Guest answers: first wash, how to dry, how to iron, how to store, colour bleeding
- Host reads three questions from chat, moderator picks them
- If chat is quiet, use the FAQ list in the moderator sheet
- Cue: "Ab dekhte hain agle 4 sarees."

7:38 Sarees S5 to S8 (2.5 minutes each)
- Same pattern as S1 to S4, but shorter. Lead with what is different from the first four
- Mention the stock of each in the first line
- Cue: "Ab doosra flash offer, ye last hai."

7:48 Flash offer 2 (S5 to S8)
- Same pattern as flash 1. Read the offer at 7:48 and 7:53
- At 7:56 say "Do minute bache hain" only if it is true
- Cue: "Ab hum samet lete hain."

7:58 Close
- Recap in three lines: what we saw, what was sold, how to order after the live
- Final CTA, next live date [date], thank the weaver

ENGAGEMENT BEATS
- 7:05 Poll: "Pehle konsa colour dekhna chahengi?" Host reads the winner at 7:06
- 7:25 Shout-out round: city names from chat, for 30 seconds
- 7:28 Q&A window opens: moderator pins three fabric-care questions
No giveaway and no paid partnership in this show. If either is added, write the rule and the disclosure here and say it on air at 7:00.

CTA 2, 7:48. "Doosra aur last flash offer. Saree S5 se S8 par [offer], code [CODE2]. Stock sirf utna hi hai jitna screen par dikh raha hai. 7:58 pe band."
